tercero-es-01.titulo: Alberto and the Secret of the Water
parrafos: Once upon a time, and two make three, bread, chocolate and coffee, there was a boy named Alberto who lived near a lake.

Every afternoon he sat on the shore to watch how the drops bounced on the water and made ripples that joined together, creating an impressive show. To him, the lake was like a friend who always had something new to show him.
One morning, when he got to the lake, he realized it was drying up. The air smelled different, as if the ground were asking for water. He ran off to see what was happening.
He noticed that, in some places, he could see the bottom of the lake. He was very scared. He thought about the fish that lived there. Where could they be?

While walking around the lake, he saw something he had never seen: a turtle trying to reach the water, but the shore had moved so far away that it was hard for her to move forward. Alberto picked her up carefully and brought her to the water.
When he got home, his mother told him that they had to save water and use only what was necessary. The lake was drying up.
They made a family plan that would help with the situation.
When Alberto took a bath, he turned off the tap while he soaped up.
His mother washed the dishes and kept the tap closed while she used the sponge.
Alberto helped clean the yard, using a rake and a broom, and no longer using the hose.
Days went by and the water level of the lake kept dropping. There was rationing.
Water came to the house only some days. Alberto helped his mother by storing water in buckets to use on the days it did not come.
They lived that way for a long time.
One afternoon, Alberto went to the lake and sat on a rock. The lake was so quiet that it seemed asleep. There were no more ripples, no shiny reflections, no fish jumping.
Alberto felt that the lake missed him as much as he missed it. “Hang in there,” he said softly. “We are doing everything we can.”
One morning they got up and it was raining hard. It rained all day.
Alberto was excited. From far away he could see the lake and how shapes formed with the ripples made by the raindrops falling on its surface. It was as if the lake were dancing with joy.
But Alberto noticed something else: The lake was full, yes… But it was also grateful.
Alberto and his mother were happy. The rationing came to an end. They were getting water every day at their house again.
They learned that water had to be conserved even when the lake was full. Because water is a treasure that, if you take care of it, always comes back.
LET'S TAKE CARE OF WATER
And they lived happily ever after. The end.
tercero-es-01.notas: Libro ilustrado: cada párrafo = una página del PDF. 'Colorín colorado, este cuento se ha acabado' es la fórmula tradicional de cierre; se tradujo con un equivalente en inglés ('And they lived happily ever after. The end.'). El original en la pág. 16 trae un guion mal colocado en el diálogo.

parrafos: My brothers and I have different assigned chores. My older brother washes the dishes. My younger brother washes and folds the laundry. I write the grocery list. I always keep my list close so I can write down what Mom tells me.

On Sunday we went to the supermarket. Before leaving home, I made sure to put the food list in my pocket. When we got there, I grabbed a basket and walked down the aisles of the supermarket. I found everything on the list except the ham. I could not see it anywhere. A store employee helped me find it.
Mom was already in the checkout line. Very carefully, I placed the cans in the shopping cart so I would not damage the bread and the eggs.
On the way home, I realized how important it is to help Mom at home. Sharing the household chores makes us feel good about ourselves.

In Puerto Rico there are many nocturnal animals. This means they eat and move around at night. The coquí is one of them. This small frog is unique to Puerto Rico and always sings at night. It also does so on rainy days and at dusk.
Bats also sleep during the day and go out to hunt for food in the dark. The ones that live in Puerto Rico eat insects, fruit, leaves, and fish.

On our island there are three nocturnal birds: the yaboa, the guabairo, and the mucarito. The yaboa is a large bird that lives in the mangroves and along riverbanks. The guabairo is a small bird that lives in dry forests. The mucarito is found in the mountain and coastal forests.
Light can affect the behavior of nocturnal animals.
That is why, when the sun goes down, it is important to turn off the lights we do not need. While people sleep, many animals begin their routine.

The Pérez family is very talented. In that family, everyone plays a musical instrument. The father plays the piano, the mother the flute, and the son the trumpet. Every afternoon you can hear what might be a party, but it is the Pérezes rehearsing.

One fine day, a neighbor knocked on the Pérezes' door to complain about the noise. Mrs. Pérez promised to make less noise so as not to bother him. Weeks went by and the rehearsals stayed the same. A group of neighbors went to the Pérezes' house asking them not to rehearse anymore.
The family decided to please the neighbors. For a long time the sound of the instruments was not heard. The afternoons were no longer cheerful. The Pérezes had stopped rehearsing.

Soon, the whole neighborhood began to miss the music. The neighbors got together and decided to go back to the Pérezes' house. This time they asked them to rehearse again. The Pérezes were thrilled with the news! That day they threw a big party, full of music and uproar.

Egypt is a country located on the African continent. The communities in this country can be very different. On one hand, we find the nobility and, of course, the pharaoh, who lived in large, beautiful palaces made of stone. On the other hand, there is the rest of the population:

they lived in small houses built with bricks made of mud and straw, called adobes. People from Egypt are called Egyptians. The pyramids were the star monuments of this great civilization, along with the sphinxes. These were built by thousands and thousands of workers and farmers. Although it was thought that the workers who took part in their construction were slaves, in reality they were farmers hired during the seasons when there was no work in the fields. Once finished, these pyramids would serve as a tomb for the pharaoh.
tercero-es-05.notas: El corte entre los dos párrafos está a mitad de frase en el original (termina en ':'); se respetó.

parrafos: Camels are fascinating animals and very important in Egypt, where they have been part of daily life and culture for thousands of years. In Egypt there are mainly two types of camels: the dromedary, which has a single hump, and the Bactrian camel, which has two humps, although the dromedary is the most common in this region.

Camels are known for their ability to survive in extreme desert conditions. They have several adaptations that allow them to live in the intense heat of the desert. For example, they can drink large amounts of water at once and store that water in their bodies. Unlike other animals, their body temperature can vary, which helps them lose less water through sweat.

In addition, their fur acts as insulation, keeping them cool during the day and warm at night. Their feet are designed for walking on hot sand, with pads that protect them. In Egypt, camels are known as “ships of the desert.” For centuries, they have been used as pack animals, carrying goods, water, and people across the vast stretches of the desert. Their endurance and ability to travel long distances make them ideal for trade along the ancient caravan routes.

Camels also have a special place in Egyptian culture. They are mentioned in ancient inscriptions and can be seen in many works of art and sculptures. They are also symbols of patience and endurance, traits valued in desert life.

Madagascar is the fourth largest island in the world, located in the Indian Ocean, off the east coast of Africa. It is separated from the African continent by the Mozambique Channel. The capital of Madagascar is Antananarivo, which is also the largest city in the country. Madagascar is famous for its incredible biodiversity.

Approximately 90% of the island's plants and animals are endemic, which means they are not found anywhere else in the world. Among its best-known species are lemurs, chameleons, and a wide variety of plants such as the baobab.

Malagasy culture is rich and diverse, influenced by African, Asian, and European traditions. Most of the population belongs to Malagasy ethnic groups, and the official language is Malagasy, although French is also widely spoken. Madagascar's economy is based on agriculture, fishing, and mining. It is one of the main producers of vanilla, and it also grows coffee, cocoa, and spices. Tourism is a growing sector, driven by biodiversity and natural beauty.

Madagascar has a rich history that includes influences from Arab explorers, European traders, and French colonization. It gained its independence from France in 1960. Madagascar faces serious environmental challenges, such as deforestation, loss of biodiversity, and climate change. Cutting down trees for farming and livestock has drastically reduced forest areas. Malagasy food is characterized by a mix of flavors and is influenced by local agriculture. Rice is a staple food, and dishes such as “romazava” (a meat and vegetable stew) are popular.

Many festivals are celebrated in Madagascar, many of them related to agriculture and tradition. The “Famadihana” is an ancestral ceremony in which families would exhume their ancestors and celebrate their memory. Madagascar has a tropical climate, with two main seasons: the rainy season (November to April) and the dry season (May to October). The island experiences a variety of climates because of its topography. Madagascar is a fascinating place with a rich cultural and natural heritage, which makes it a unique destination in the world.

On a beautiful morning in Madagascar, a friendly lemur named Lio was leaping from branch to branch. Lio was known for his great curiosity and his love of making new friends. He loved living among the colorful trees and enjoying the birdsong, but he had a big dream: to travel beyond the island to discover the world.
One day, while playing with his friends the chameleons, Lio exclaimed excitedly:
“I want to see more than just our jungle! I want to know other lands, other cultures. Who is coming with me?”
His friends looked at him with surprise and a little fear.
“But how are you going to do that, Lio? The jungle is our home, we are safe here!” said one of the female chameleons, trembling with excitement.
But Lio was not discouraged. He knew that if he wanted to explore, he needed a strategy. So he went to his wise friend, the old tortoise, Don Torto.
“Don Torto, is it possible for a lemur like me to explore beyond Madagascar?”
The old tortoise smiled and answered:
“Of course, little friend. With courage and preparation, you can go wherever you want. But don't forget: adventure is more fun with friends.
Do you have any who would like to go with you?”
Lio lit up.
“Yes! I will call all my friends from the jungle and together we will form an expedition!”
That is how Lio began to plan his trip. He called together his friends: the cheerful zebra, the swift gazelle, and the clever parrot. They were all excited, but also worried.
“What if we get lost?” asked the gazelle, her heart pounding with excitement.
“Don't worry. I have a map!” said Lio, very proudly. The night before leaving, the friends gathered. Lio, excited, said to them:
“Tomorrow our adventure begins! We will discover new lands and make new friends. Remember, always together, like a team.”
At dawn, the group said goodbye to their home and set out on the road. They passed through mountains and rivers, enjoying every moment.
They met a mythical flamingo who made them laugh and a group of dolphins that swam around them. But one afternoon, while crossing a dense forest, they ran into a problem.
“Oh no! The map got wet and it can't be read!” exclaimed the parrot, as everyone began to worry.
Lio felt fear taking over, but he remembered Don Torto's words, so he gathered his courage.
“Don't despair, friends. Even if we don't have the map, we have something more important: we have each other!”
Using his wits, Lio suggested:

“Why don't we split into small groups? That way each group can explore a part of the forest and find the way. Then we meet back here, at this big tree. And if anyone finds something valuable, let me know!”
His friends nodded, taking heart from Lio's words.

Finally, thanks to the understanding and unity of the group, they found the way back and, toward sunset, they reached the northern beach, a place they had never imagined. They were all tired, but the excitement of having faced the challenge together gave them energy.
“We did it!” shouted the zebra, jumping for joy.
“It was the effort of teamwork, Lio. Thank you for being so brave!” said the gazelle.
Lio smiled and looked at his friends.
“Never forget that together we are always stronger. And now, let's enjoy this wonderful beach!”
They spent the afternoon playing in the waves and discovering little shells. When the sun began to set, Lio felt his heart overflowing with happiness.
“This trip is only the beginning. There is so much more to discover, there is a whole world waiting for us!” he said.

With hearts full of joy and new stories to tell, Lio and his friends returned to Madagascar. They learned that adventure is more enriching when you share it, and that with courage and teamwork, no goal is impossible. From then on, Lio the lemur became the best explorer of his jungle, and every time he looked at the horizon, he knew that new adventures awaited them, one after another, all waiting to be discovered.
And so, under the glow of the moon, Lio imagined his next destination, with a big smile on his face.

Once upon a time there was a fox walking through the forest when she saw a crow perched on a branch, with a piece of cheese in his beak. The cheese gleamed in the sun, and the fox, who was very hungry, thought about how to get it.
The fox, cunning as always, decided to use her wits to trick the crow. She went up to the tree and, looking at the crow with a smile, said to him:
“How handsome you are, friend crow! What bright and elegant feathers! I am sure you are the king of all the birds, the noblest and wisest.
If your song is as beautiful as your looks, there is no doubt that the whole forest must admire you.”
The crow, flattered by the praise, puffed up with pride. No one had ever said such nice things to him before. He believed that if the fox thought so highly of him, his song must be just as wonderful.
“Listen to my song, dear fox!” said the crow, opening his beak to sing.
But just at that moment, the piece of cheese fell from his beak and was quickly snatched up by the cunning fox.
The fox, with a satisfied smile, said to the crow:
“There is no doubt that you are a king of the skies, but remember that he who talks the most does not always have the most. Next time, don't let flattery make you forget what matters most.”
The crow, ashamed, looked down at the ground, regretting that he had lost his cheese by letting himself be carried away by praise.
tercero-es-09.notas: En el original el párrafo 2 es el primer diálogo, partido en dos párrafos (2 y 3).

parrafos: Christmas is one of the most celebrated holidays in Spain. Cities and towns are decorated with Christmas lights and ornaments, and families get together to share a big meal. One of the most important traditions is Christmas Eve, when a special dinner is held with typical dishes such as turrón (an almond sweet) and roast lamb.

Christmas Eve (December 24) is one of the most important nights of the Christmas festivities in Puerto Rico. It is an occasion to share with family and friends, and to celebrate the birth of Jesus in an atmosphere of joy and faith. Families gather for a special dinner, which is a moment of great tradition.

However, the most awaited day is Three Kings Day (January 6), when children receive gifts from the Three Kings (Melchior, Caspar, and Balthazar), who represent the three wise men who traveled to Bethlehem to bring gifts to the baby Jesus. The night before, in many cities, the Three Kings Parades are held, a procession full of floats, music, and, of course, candy. Three Kings Day is just as important in Puerto Rico. In many families, especially in rural areas, children put shoeboxes filled with grass under the bed or at the foot of the Christmas tree so the Three Kings will leave them gifts. It is a date full of joy, when festivities are also enjoyed.
tercero-es-10.notas: El texto mezcla tradiciones de España y de Puerto Rico, como en el original.

parrafos: The maga tree was proclaimed the national tree of Puerto Rico in 1956. This tree, whose scientific name is Thespesia grandiflora, is native to the island and has bright purple flowers that are greatly admired for their beauty. The maga symbolizes the island's native flora and natural wealth. Its symbolism is linked to the identity and love of nature of Puerto Ricans, and it is a common figure in the literature and cultural representations of the island.
The cheese rolls, proud and swift,
like a golden lightning bolt that defies the wind,
and the hill sings its mischievous laughter,
creaking beneath the steps of the brave.
The runners leap and thrash about,
an army of shadows seeking glory,
and the wind whispers in their ears:
“Run, run, run!” in an endless echo.
The wheel rolls and echoes,
crack, crack! each blow, a challenge,
a thunder of cheese that does not stop,
beneath the sky that throbs with excitement.
tercero-es-12.notas: Poema: traducción literal, no conserva la rima.

parrafos: Once upon a time, deep in the mountains of China, there was a big, fluffy panda named Bao. Bao was a very special bear, with black and white fur that made him look as if he were always wearing an elegant suit.

Bao preferred to lead a solitary life, but he was still very content and happy. Every morning he got up early and stretched his arms and legs. Then he climbed down from the tall bamboo where he slept and went to look for breakfast. Bamboo was his favorite food and he could eat it all day long. Bao had a digestive system especially adapted to process this tough, fibrous plant.

After breakfast, Bao spent some time exploring his surroundings. He loved strolling through the dense bamboo forests, climbing over rocky ground, and crossing shallow streams. He was always looking for new patches of bamboo to feed on.

When the day got warmer, Bao took a nap in the shade of a tree. He slept for a while, dreaming of all the bamboo he planned to eat for dinner. When the day got warmer, Bao took a nap in the shade of a tree. He slept for a while, dreaming of all the bamboo he planned to eat for dinner.
After the nap, Bao spent the rest of the afternoon eating bamboo and enjoying the peace and quiet of the mountain. He gazed at the beautiful sunset while resting in his favorite spot.
At night, Bao climbed back up the bamboo to sleep. He felt safe and protected high up in the trees, and he could hear the relaxing sound of the wind whispering through the bamboo leaves.

Bao's life was simple but very happy. He had plenty of delicious food, a beautiful, peaceful home in the mountains, and he felt content living a solitary life, never needing more than what nature provided.
tercero-es-13.notas: El párrafo 3 del original repite dos veces las mismas dos oraciones; se tradujo fielmente y conviene corregirlo en el texto fuente.

tercero-es-14.titulo: Little Ravi and the Light of Diwali
parrafos: Once upon a time there was a boy named Ravi who lived in a small village in India. Ravi was a very curious boy, always exploring his surroundings and asking about his family's traditions. His favorite holiday was Diwali, the Festival of Lights, which they celebrated every year.

As Diwali drew near, Ravi was excited. His mother explained that Diwali symbolized the victory of light over darkness and good over evil. During this festival, people decorated their homes with lights and flowers, and shared sweets with friends and family.
One day, while helping his mother prepare the sweets, Ravi noticed that his neighbor, old Mr. Patel, had not decorated his house.
Worried, Ravi decided to visit him.
“Hello, Mr. Patel!” said Ravi, smiling. “Why haven't you gotten your house ready for Diwali?”
Mr. Patel sighed and answered: “I don't have many lights or the energy to decorate. This year, I feel a little sad.”
Ravi thought for a moment. Then he had a bright idea.
“I can help you!” he exclaimed. Together, they began to decorate Mr. Patel's house. Ravi brought lights from his home and some flowers too. Soon, the old man's house shone like never before.
As they worked, Ravi asked Mr. Patel about his memories of Diwali.
“When I was young, Diwali was a time of joy and togetherness,” the old man told him. “The family would gather and we would share stories under the lights.”
Ravi listened carefully, feeling how Mr. Patel's story lit up his heart.

Finally, the night of Diwali arrived. The village filled with lights and laughter. Ravi and Mr. Patel joined their neighbors in the square, where everyone lit candles and firecrackers. But the most special moment came when Ravi took the old man to his house, where his family had prepared a big dinner.
“Thank you, Ravi,” said Mr. Patel with tears of joy. “Today you have reminded me of the importance of community and friendship.”

Ravi smiled, feeling that he had done something valuable. That night, as the lights of Diwali lit up the sky, Ravi understood that true light came not only from lamps, but from the love and kindness we share with others.
And so, Ravi and Mr. Patel celebrated an unforgettable Diwali, full of laughter, friendship, and, above all, light in their hearts.

Once upon a time there was a boy named Alexei who lived in a small village in Russia, surrounded by vast fields and snow-covered mountains. Alexei was a dreamer, always imagining adventures and explorations in the nature around him.

One day, while walking in the nearby forest, Alexei heard a strange sound coming from behind some bushes. As he got closer, he saw a little fox caught in a trap. Its eyes were sad and frightened. Alexei, who had always loved animals, felt deep empathy for the little fox.
“Don't worry, little friend,” Alexei whispered. “I will help you.”

Very carefully, Alexei managed to free the fox from the trap. The animal, though scared, stayed still, looking at him with gratitude. Then, to Alexei's surprise, the fox gave him a small nudge with its snout, as if thanking him from the heart. Then, with an agile leap, the fox disappeared among the trees. That night, Alexei had a wonderful dream. In his dream, the fox appeared again, but this time it was not alone. At its side were other animals of the forest: a wise owl, a playful hare, and an elegant deer. The fox spoke to him:
“Thank you for saving me, Alexei. Tonight, I will take you to a magical place.”

The fox guided him to a moonlit clearing, where all the animals were gathering to celebrate. There was music and laughter, and the air was full of joy. Alexei joined them, dancing and playing. In that place, he felt free and happy, surrounded by friends.

When Alexei woke up, he felt that the dream had been more than just an illusion. He decided he had to do something special for the animals of the forest. So he began to collect food and leave it near his house, making sure there was always something for those who could not find enough in winter. As the days went by, Alexei saw that the animals began to come closer, leaving tracks in the snow and enjoying the treats he had left. One day, the fox appeared again, and this time it stayed close to him, like a loyal companion. From that moment on, Alexei and the fox became inseparable friends. Together they explored the forest, discovering new trails and sharing many adventures. Alexei learned to care for and respect animals, and every day their friendship grew stronger.
